title: Scattering-based detection of fungal spores on a photonic integrated platform: an ASCA-assisted proof-of-concept study
abstract: Airborne fungal pathogens, such as Penicillium expansum, pose a severe threat to post-harvest crop preservation and food safety, demanding rapid and reliable detection methods. This study presents a photonic integrated sensing platform, based on Ge-Se-Te RIB optical waveguides, as a proof-of-concept for the discrimination of fungal spores under controlled laboratory conditions in the short-wave infrared (SWIR) range. To evaluate the performance of the sensor over a comprehensive 45-day experimental campaign, Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations were combined with advanced chemometric analysis. FEM modeling confirmed the evanescent field interaction with micrometer-sized spores on the waveguide surface. To extract the subtle biological signal resulting from high-density spore deposition from dominant system drifts and environmental noise, ANOVA-Simultaneous Component Analysis (ASCA) was applied to the multidimensional spectral data. ASCA successfully isolated the specific variance related to spore deposition, even though it accounted for only 0.2% of the global variance. These results highlight the potential of combining chalcogenide waveguide technologies with ASCA-driven analytics for scattering-based, label-free bio-sensing applications, paving the way toward future quantitative and species-selective developments in the mid-wave infrared (MWIR).

title: yancc: A GPU-accelerated, differentiable solver for neoclassical transport in tokamaks and stellarators
abstract: We present yancc, a new GPU-accelerated solver for the drift kineticequation that computes neoclassical transport fluxes, flows, and currents intokamaks and stellarators. The drift kinetic equation is challenging to solvenumerically due to strong advection-dominance, recirculating flows, internalboundary layers, severe anisotropy, and high dimensionality. Fast and accuratesolutions to the drift kinetic equation are required for high fidelity optimization,profile prediction, and analysis of experiments with uncertainty quantification.yancc solves both the full four-dimensional drift kinetic equation (retainingspeed-dependent collisions, energy scattering, and full interspeciescoupling), and the reduced monoenergetic form. The discretization combines aMaxwell polynomial collocation grid in speed with finite differences in pitch angleand the flux surface coordinates, using a modified upwind stencil designed toimprove diagonal dominance for multigrid efficiency. The resulting linearsystem is solved with a multigrid-preconditioned Krylov method. Built in JAX,yancc is fully differentiable, enabling gradient-based optimization andadjoint sensitivity analysis. Benchmarks against MONKES and SFINCS showagreement within 1\% across a range of collisionalities, geometries, andmulti-species configurations. yancc achieves roughly an order of magnitudespeedup over SFINCS on a per-scan basis while using an order of magnitude lessmemory, with runtime remaining nearly flat across the full range ofcollisionality.

DNA-BFN: Bayesian Flow Networks for Generative Modeling of Regulatory DNA Sequences.
abstract: MOTIVATION Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. RESULTS Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. AVAILABILITY The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Niclosamide Suppresses Osteoclastogenesis and Bone Resorption: Involvement of STAT3 Signaling
abstract: Niclosamide, known for its anticancer and anti-inflammatory effects via modulation of NF-κB and STAT3 signaling, has now been shown to suppress osteoclast differentiation and function through STAT3 inhibition. In vitro experiments demonstrated that niclosamide downregulates STAT3 activation, leading to reduced expression of genes involved in osteoclast differentiation, acid secretion, chemotaxis, and pyroptosis, thereby impairing multiple osteoclast biological behaviors. In vivo, niclosamide treatment attenuated bone loss in an ovariectomy-induced mouse model of osteoporosis by inhibiting osteoclast activity. The STAT3 activator colivelin partially reversed these niclosamide-induced effects on bone metabolism. Collectively, niclosamide inhibits both osteoclast formation and the bone-resorptive function of mature osteoclasts via suppression of the STAT3 pathway, suggesting a novel therapeutic approach for osteoporosis.

title: Strange attractors: purpose, synchronicity, flow, and the neurodynamics of meaning
abstract: This paper proposes a neurodynamic framework for meaningful experience, grounded in the recursive alignment of brain dynamics across time. We argue that the meaningful experiences known as “purpose”, “synchronicity”, and “flow” are not distinct phenomena, but temporal expressions of the same underlying process: metastable coherence in the brain’s attractor landscape. Synchronicity marks transient realignments across representational levels; flow reflects the low-entropy navigation of emergent structures; and purpose encodes long-term integration into causal agency of a self-model. Drawing on active inference, dynamical systems theory, and recent work on predictive processing and memory consolidation, we formalize these states as trajectories through phase-space—differentiated by temporal depth, stability, and precision-weighting. We offer empirical predictions for each regime, linking neural signatures such as sharp-wave ripples, P300b activity, and network coherence to experiential markers of meaning. We also propose a developmental interpretation informed by Robert Kegan’s subject–object theory, framing purpose as an evolving attractor shaped through recursive narrative and identity updating. This model suggests that meaning is not only symbolic or semantic, but dynamic, embodied, and experimentally testable: a measurable function of the brain’s capacity to coordinate across nested timescales.

title: MRI-Based Machine Learning to Differentiate True Progression from Pseudoprogression in Glioblastoma: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND Differentiating true progression (TP) from pseudoprogression (PsP) after chemoradiation for glioblastoma remains clinically difficult. We evaluated externally validated diagnostic performance of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based machine learning models and appraised study quality and transparency. METHODS PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and Cochrane Library were searched through October 1, 2025 (PROSPERO registration CRD420251144894). Eligible adult glioblastoma studies used MRI-based machine learning to distinguish TP from PsP against histopathology and/or clinicoradiologic follow-up. The primary meta-analysis included external test cohorts with extractable 2 × 2 data; internal and combined internal and external test analyses were secondary. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with bivariate random-effects models. RESULTS Thirty-one studies including 2,344 patients undergoing imaging assessment were included. Seven external test cohorts, including 219 patient observations, entered the primary meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.63-0.88), specificity was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.63-0.84), and summary area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.81 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.69-0.91). Internal test cohorts showed higher apparent performance than external cohorts (AUC, 0.91 vs 0.81), but the difference was not statistically significant (difference, -0.09; 95% CI, -0.22 to 0.02; P = 0.12). Risk of bias was frequently high or unclear, and reporting transparency was heterogeneous. CONCLUSIONS MRI-based machine learning showed moderate-to-good external validation performance for TP-versus-PsP discrimination, but evidence remains limited by small external test cohorts, bias, and incomplete reporting. Larger transparent multicenter validations are needed before routine clinical implementation.

title: Navigating intentions: exploring the cognitive and environmental drivers of productive and destructive entrepreneurial intentions
abstract: This study aims to understand how entrepreneurial effort is allocated by differentiating between productive and destructive pathways. It examines how cognitive drivers (attitudes, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control) and environmental valuations (trust-based networks and status incentives) interact to steer entrepreneurship students toward value-creating or value-destructive entrepreneurial intentions in an emerging economy marked by institutional complexity. Building on an integrated framework that synthesizes the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with institutional and social capital theories, we developed and tested a dual-pathway structural model. We collected data from 783 entrepreneurship students across nine Iranian universities. We used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to test two separate models for productive and destructive entrepreneurial intentions. Core TPB relationships were supported for both pathways, but critical asymmetries emerged. Closeness valuation significantly strengthened attitudes toward productive entrepreneurship but did not influence the destructive pathway. Social valuation played a dual role: promoting productive intentions by strengthening perceived control and norms, while also inhibiting destructive intentions. Formal testing of comparative hypotheses revealed that attitude and subjective norms were significantly stronger drivers of destructive intention, while perceived behavioral control was more influential for productive intention. The study unpacks entrepreneurial intention into distinct ethical pathways, introducing a dual-pathway model specifying how identical environmental factors produce opposing effects depending on a venture's ethical valence. It provides rare empirical evidence from Iran's understudied entrepreneurial ecosystem and demonstrates how institutional voids shape intention pathways. The findings offer actionable guidance for educators and policymakers designing entrepreneurship education interventions that cultivate productive entrepreneurship while mitigating destructive practices in emerging economies.

title: Corporate ethical and responsible AI (CERAi) and AI trustworthiness: a lifecycle perspective and empirical insights
abstract: This study develops and empirically validates a Corporate Ethical and Responsible AI (CERAi) lifecycle framework. The framework comprises three interdependent stages: design and development, testing and training, and deployment and usage. The study aims to move the research beyond abstract principles and policy analyses toward empirically grounded, lifecycle-integrated artificial intelligence AI governance theory. It positions ethical AI and responsible AI governance as the two constitutive components of the CERAi construct, and AI trustworthiness as a conceptually and empirically distinct downstream outcome anchored in stage-specific organizational governance mechanisms. The CERAi framework is scoped broadly to encompass governance of both conventional/traditional machine learning models and autonomous AI agents operating within organizational settings. We administered a large-scale survey to 500 attendees at a national AI conference in the United States in early 2026, yielding 143 useable responses from AI professionals across healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, retail and energy sectors. We developed and validated multi-item scales for each CERAi lifecycle stage using established ethical AI and AI governance frameworks. Structural equation modeling was employed to assess the measurement model and to test both direct path hypotheses and mediation hypotheses. Both CERAIi design and development and CERAi deployment and usage have significant positive direct effects on AI trustworthiness, whereas CERAi testing and training do not. Our results also indicate a significant serial mediation pathway in which CERAi deployment and usage enhance AI trustworthiness through testing and training, followed by design and development. Conversely, testing and training alone do not mediate the relationship between deployment and usage and AI trustworthiness, indicating that design-stage ethics serve as an intervening (mediating) mechanism through which governance activity enacted at later lifecycle stages is associated with perceived AI trustworthiness. This is consistent with testing and training's association with trustworthiness operating indirectly, mediated by the ethical architecture established during the design and development stage. Findings of this study demonstrate that AI trustworthiness reflects differentiated perceived salience across AI lifecycle stages, whereby stakeholders appear to weight visible, deployment-stage governance more heavily than upstream design and testing stage governance in forming trustworthiness judgments, rather than reflecting a definitive validation that governance effects accumulate uniformly across all stages in isolation. This study makes a distinctive contribution by providing empirical evidence for a governance-sequencing mechanism, whereby design-stage ethics function as a mediating pathway shaping the effectiveness of governance activity at later lifecycle stages. To the best of our knowledge, such a mediated, stage-sequential mechanism has not previously been demonstrated using primary data within a comprehensive, three-stage CERAi lifecycle framework linking organizational ethical and responsible governance practices to AI trustworthiness outcomes.

title: Beyond usefulness: cognitive and emotional correlates of AI use intentions among HR professionals
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human resource management (HRM), yet the cognitive and psychological factors associated with human resource (HR) professionals’ intentions to use AI remain incompletely understood. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and appraisal perspectives, this study examines the relative associations of Cognitive Evaluation, AI-Use Anxiety, AI-Related Job Insecurity, organizational AI use across HR functions, and AI Knowledge with behavioral intention to use AI. It also explores whether AI Knowledge moderates these relationships. Survey data were collected from 285 HR professionals. Confirmatory factor analyses assessed the measurement structure of the study constructs, followed by hierarchical moderated regression analyses examining their unique associations with behavioral intention and the exploratory moderating role of AI Knowledge. Cognitive Evaluation, reflecting perceived usefulness and ease of use, showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention to use AI. AI-Use Anxiety demonstrated a smaller negative association, whereas AI-Related Job Insecurity, AI Use Across HR Functions, and AI Knowledge did not explain significant unique variance once the competing predictors were considered simultaneously. The comprehensive model explained 66.8% of the variance in behavioral intention. The exploratory interaction analyses provided no clear evidence that AI Knowledge systematically moderated the relationships examined. Organizations implementing AI in HR should address both employees’ evaluations of the technology and apprehension surrounding its use. Implementation strategies should demonstrate the practical usefulness and usability of AI through role-specific examples, hands-on training, and opportunities to experiment with AI tools in realistic HR contexts. Organizations should also recognize AI-use anxiety as a distinct potential barrier by providing accessible support, low-risk opportunities for familiarization, and clear communication throughout implementation. These strategies may help create conditions that support employees’ willingness to use AI. This study extends research on AI use intentions by examining cognitive, emotional, knowledge-related, and organizational-exposure factors simultaneously rather than in isolation. The findings show that HR professionals’ intentions to use AI are most strongly associated with evaluations of its usefulness and usability, while AI-use anxiety represents a smaller but distinct negative correlate. By distinguishing AI-use anxiety from AI-related job insecurity and individual AI knowledge from organizational AI exposure, the study provides a more differentiated account of the factors associated with HR professionals’ intentions to use AI.

title: The dynamics of knowledge transfer and retention in entrepreneurial education: a conceptual exploration of enabling technologies
abstract: This conceptual paper aims to examine Entrepreneurial Education (EE) in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) through a Knowledge Management (KM) lens. It explains how enabling technology affordances, when aligned with the characteristics of entrepreneurial knowledge, shape Knowledge Transfer (KT) and Knowledge Retention (KR) under conditions of cognitive bias. It clarifies how KM processes support durable entrepreneurial capability development. The study adopts a theory-driven conceptual methodology. Drawing on KM process theory and conceptual theory-building guidance, the paper develops a mechanism-based framework through six stages: problematisation, theoretical anchoring, construct selection, mechanism mapping, model integration and proposition development. The framework positions KT and KR as the analytical core, enabling technologies as differentiated KM affordances, and cognitive bias as an embedded condition that can distort knowledge interpretation, transfer, retention and reuse. The framework proposes that enabling technologies can strengthen KT and KR when their affordances align with the knowledge’s tacitness, codifiability and contextual dependence, and are supported by interaction, reflection, curation and governance routines. Immersive/simulation, AI/analytics and collaborative/process technologies support KT/KR mechanisms. Cognitive bias can weaken or distort knowledge transfer, retention and reuse, whereas bias-aware routines and cohort-to-cohort feedback can improve knowledge fidelity, programme memory and entrepreneurial capability development. The paper advances a KM-centred reframing of EE by positioning KT and KR as the focal mechanisms linking enabling technologies to durable entrepreneurial capability development. It differentiates technologies by their KM affordances and integrates cognitive bias, boundary conditions and programme-level feedback within a single conceptual architecture, offering testable propositions and design principles for technology-enabled EE.

Carbon Accumulation in Tropical Dry Forests and Savannas Despite Widespread Land‐Cover Change, Revealed by Radar Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate mapping of woody biomass and its temporal change is critical for understanding the global carbon balance, informing restoration and supporting evidence‐based policy on climate mitigation and livelihoods. The vegetation of the dry tropics, comprised largely of dry forests and savannas, holds substantial woody carbon stocks, but both stocks and change over time remain uncertain. Where Earth Observation (EO) data have been used to estimate change over time, different products give conflicting results on the direction, magnitude and location of change. We present pan‐dry‐tropical maps of aboveground carbon density (AGCD) and AGCD change at 100 m resolution for the years 2015–2024, developed using ALOS ScanSAR satellite radar observations calibrated with in situ measurements ( n = 237). These maps suggest an aboveground woody carbon pool (AGC) in the dry tropics of 25.3 2.0 PgC, ~13.0% of global AGC. Net AGC has increased by 0.43 0.07 PgC yr −1 , ~20.0% of the global net land sink. The overall net increase (0.43 PgC yr −1 ) is comprised of gross losses from deforestation and degradation (0.27 0.05 PgC yr −1 ) and gains due to densification and extensification of 0.59 0.1 PgC yr −1 , with the balance accounted for by small changes (change < 20% of AGCD; 0.11 PgC yr −1 ). Losses are equally split between degradation and deforestation, while gains are divided roughly 2:1 between the densification of woody ecosystems and expansion into previously grass‐dominated areas. These new maps, created with a dry‐tropics‐specific EO method, highlight the importance of tropical dry forests and savannas in the global carbon cycle. The prominent role of degradation‐related losses suggests that climate change mitigation will need to focus much more on reducing losses from overharvesting than at present. The widespread increases in carbon density and the increase in tree biomass into open systems present major challenges for biodiversity conservation, restoration and livelihoods.

title: Thermal Generalism Shapes Tolerance to Extreme Heatwaves in Estuarine Fishes
abstract: Climate change is widely expected to push many taxa beyond their biological limits, yet some populations persist in environments that routinely experience climatic extremes. This raises a fundamental question: does their thermal tolerance reflect species‐level thermal generalism (an evolved capacity to maintain performance across a broad thermal range) or population‐specific acclimation to local conditions (phenotypic plasticity)? Distinguishing between these alternatives is key for predicting whether tolerance to climatic extremes will generalise across species distributions or remain restricted to heat‐tolerant populations. To test these competing hypotheses, we quantified physiological performance (at cellular and organismal levels) in three economically important estuarine fish ( Acanthopagrus australis , Sillago ciliata and Rhabdosargus sarba ) collected from 20 sites across 15 estuaries along a ~1000‐km latitudinal gradient spanning their core and poleward range edges. Sites differed in thermal variability, including some that intermittently exceeded the severest end‐of‐century climate projections. We then experimentally exposed two of the fish species from low and high thermal variability sites to moderate (+2°C, 14 days) or extreme (+4°C, 7 days) simulated marine heatwave events, assessing 12 physiological and behavioural proxies. All three species collected in situ maintained comparable physiological performance across sites of contrasting thermal variability. Both experimental species, each collected from a single high‐ and low‐variability site, tolerated heatwave conditions regardless of thermal history or heatwave intensity, supporting species‐level thermal generalism rather than population‐specific acclimation. In the absence of heatwave conditions, S. ciliata from high‐variability sites also showed steeper allometric scaling and faster growth at 26 versus 24°C experimental control temperatures, suggesting this species may benefit from the warmer baseline temperatures projected under gradual climate change. Combined, our findings support thermal generalism as the primary driver of tolerance in estuarine fishes to climatic extremes, with important implications for the fisheries they support under climate change.

title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
abstract: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.

title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
abstract: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.

title: Application of ALADIN model outputs for solid precipitation forecasting and detection
abstract: Meteorological services face a major challenge in providing reliable snowfall forecasts and detecting solid precipitation, as precise data is needed for weather warnings, damage assessments, hydrological modeling, and many other tasks. This study evaluates the skill of the ALADIN numerical weather prediction model in solid precipitation forecasting at 126 stations of the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute (CHMI) between August 2019 and July 2025. Model performance was assessed against quality-controlled human present weather observations using common verification metrics, including the Probability of Detection (POD), False Alarm Ratio (FAR), Critical Success Index (CSI), and Heidke Skill Score (HSS). Further, the ALADIN_SN weighted index of solid precipitation occurrence was assimilated from ALADIN snow forecasts in hourly intervals using two sets of empirical lead-time-dependent weights. During the snow season, ALADIN_SN showed a mean POD of 0.68, FAR of 0.48, and HSS of 0.53, with an overall accuracy exceeding 83% at all stations. Air temperature is the most important variable affecting the model performance, with better results at temperatures below approximately +2°C. The skill of ALADIN_SN also improved with increasing solid precipitation intensity and duration. Case studies demonstrated that ALADIN_SN successfully captured large-scale snowfall events associated with synoptic systems but struggled with localized or short-lived precipitation and phase transitions at temperatures above freezing, and it often overestimated the spatial extent of solid precipitation zones. Overall, the ALADIN_SN parameter provides a spatially consistent, computationally efficient, and operationally feasible method for identifying solid precipitation occurrence, suitable for supplementing networks of automated measurement systems and human weather observers.

title: Genetically Defined Acute Myeloid Leukemia Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell Clones Reveal Selective Impairment of Hematopoietic Development.
Living on borrowed oxygen in the goldenrod gall fly (Eurosta solidaginis).
abstract: Hypoxia in plant tissue should affect animals living within them. Gall makers stimulate their plant hosts to produce the gall they inhabit and feed on, and also influence the gall phenotype for other adaptations, such as defence against predators. In the context of adapting to potential gall hypoxia through the extended phenotype of the gall, we studied the prevalence and conditions leading to hypoxia in goldenrod galls induced by Eurosta solidaginis. Larval respirometry data showed only mild tolerance to hypoxia, based on elevated critical oxygen partial pressures (∼10 kPa). Mathematical modelling of gas diffusion into the gall suggested that the extent of prevalent hypoxia is tolerable to the larva, while more severe temporary hypoxia may occur early in the host plant's growth season. As galls mature, the cortex layer that makes up most of the gall volume becomes less metabolically active and more permeable to gas diffusion, which is important in preventing severe hypoxia. While the mature cortex layer is unlikely to have been specifically an adaptation to hypoxia, it could mitigate the need for other trade-offs in gas exchange. Since gall makers can influence gall size and tissue composition, this raises the possibility that, on top of the already established predation trade-offs, the gall maker must balance the hypoxia risk of remaining in less differentiated, cytoplasm-rich tissue with the costs associated with inducing a larger, more mature gall with greater gas diffusion capacity.

title: Beyond the Thin-Layer Limit: Differentiable Volumetric Training for Visible-Range Diffractive Neural Networks
A Bioinformatics Data Platform on Snowflake Using Life-Science Ontologies as Context for AI Agents
abstract: Life-science ontologies describe concepts such as genes, phenotypes, diseases, and chemical entities under shared identifiers and hierarchies, and over a quarter of a century they have become a foundation for annotation and analysis in bioinformatics. AI agents now assemble research procedures on their own, choosing and running databases and analysis tools, and how well they work depends on the definitions of meaning they can consult, that is, on the context layer. In enterprise data platforms, this layer is increasingly built as an organization-internal operational ontology, as exemplified by Palantir, whereas reference ontologies in the life sciences are maintained by communities outside any single organization. Using Snowflake as an example, we discuss an architecture composed of semantic views that define the meaning of internal data, Cortex Agent that queries through them, and custom tools and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that reach external ontologies. The results of concept resolution and mapping obtained from outside are stored by a custom tool in tables within Snowflake for each query, and are joined with internal data under the semantic view and under the same access control. Taking target–disease matching in drug discovery and cohort definition in real-world data as hypothetical use cases, we show, as a conceptual design, that the set of entities to be matched changes with how far the ontology hierarchy is traversed, and that the temporal conditions of a cohort are applied to the same records as the concept set obtained from the ontology.

title: Adapting Vision Foundation Models with Synthetic Data for Open-Pit Mining Crack Segmentation
abstract: Automatic crack segmentation in open-pit mining is constrained by the scarcity of representative, labeled datasets. Vision foundation models (VFMs) offer transferable visual representations, but their training-free performance on mining imagery and the benefits of synthetic-only adaptation remain insufficiently established. This study evaluates training-free VFM pipelines and investigates whether synthetic supervision improves their transfer to real-world crack imagery. SynthMineCrack is introduced as a diverse open-pit mining crack dataset, supporting model training and hyperparameter selection without real imagery or manual annotations. SAM 3 is adapted using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), layer normalization (LN) tuning, and adapters, individually and jointly, and compared with task-specific models trained on the same synthetic data. Evaluation on both in- and out-of-domain datasets shows that SAM 3 achieves the strongest training-free performance, while joint adaptation of all three operators improves intersection-over-union (IoU) on the mining evaluation dataset by 18.25 percentage points (pp). This configuration achieves a mean IoU of 69.39% across the five datasets, exceeding SegFormer, the strongest task-specific model, by 10.77 pp. Diagnostic analyses associate these gains with more complete crack recovery while the pretrained visual representation remains largely preserved. This configuration updates only 0.326% of the instantiated model’s parameter count and incurs little additional inference overhead. Together, these findings support synthetic-only adaptation as a practical means of improving SAM 3 for real-world crack segmentation while retaining inference requirements close to those of the base model.

title: Short-Term Traffic Prediction: From Statistical Models to Spatial-Temporal Deep Learning
abstract: Short-term traffic prediction (STTP) is a core component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), supporting proactive traffic management, congestion mitigation, and reliable traveler information. This review synthesizes the methodological evolution of STTP from classical statistical approaches to modern spatio-temporal deep learning. Its literature is organized according to the principal modeling capabilities required by traffic forecasting: temporal dynamics, nonlinear relationships, spatial dependencies, network topology, and long-range interactions. Statistical models, classical machine learning, recurrent and convolutional neural networks, graph-based spatio-temporal models, transformer-based architectures, and hybrid frameworks are compared with respect to prediction horizon, network scale, interpretability, computational burden, and deployment feasibility. The synthesis indicates that important recent gains arise from explicitly representing spatial structure jointly with temporal dynamics, rather than from increasingly complex temporal models alone. At the same time, higher predictive capacity often introduces costs in training, inference, interpretability, and data dependence. The review therefore frames contemporary STTP as an accuracy-complexity-deployability trade-off and identifies open directions in scalable graph learning, uncertainty-aware forecasting, explainability, heterogeneous-data integration, and real-time/edge deployment. Because reported metrics are not directly comparable across studies with different datasets and experimental protocols, the review emphasizes qualitative evidence and modeling capability rather than unsupported cross-study numerical rankings.

title: Adaptive Long-range UAV Flight Planning using Monte Carlo Search Trees
abstract: Long-range fixed-wing UAV missions require energy-efficient, dynamically feasible trajectories that can adapt online to evolving wind and airspace constraints. We present a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based framework that addresses this challenge by formulating mission planning as a finite-horizon Markov decision process incorporating aircraft kinematics, onboard energy dynamics, forecast wind fields, terrain, and time-varying no-fly zones. The MCTS planner searches over waypoint references generated by pre-stabilizing feedback controllers and a constraint-aware navigation field, yielding dynamically feasible trajectories. Simulation results from medical delivery scenarios show that the MCTS planner outperforms baseline geometric planners and population-based optimization algorithms. Moreover, the MCTS planner can be used in closed-loop to rapidly compute safe diversion trajectories under evolving constraints.

title: Multi-Crop Irrigation Need Classification Based on Machine Learning with an Indonesian-Language GenAI-UX Recommendation Layer
abstract: Inefficient irrigation water use remains a critical challenge in Indonesian agriculture, and the complexity of raw sensor data hinders adoption by smallholder farmers who lack data-analysis skills. This study develops an intelligent irrigation Decision Support System that integrates interpretable Machine Learning with an Indonesian-language GenAI-UX recommendation layer, using a publicly available multi-crop irrigation scheduling dataset (501 records, nine crops) with an analytical focus on paddy and maize. Four components are combined into one pipeline: (i) irrigation-need classification compared across six algorithms; (ii) regression of a continuous water-requirement score; (iii) sensor-anomaly detection using Isolation Forest cross-validated with the Interquartile Range method; and (iv) a rule-based natural-language recommendation layer whose operating point is optimized by a Genetic Algorithm. Validity was safeguarded through stratified five-fold cross-validation and leakage-controlled preprocessing. Gradient Boosting achieved the best classification performance (F1-score 0.980; cross-validated F1 0.963), Random Forest Regressor reached R square of 0.807, Isolation Forest agreed with IQR outliers at 95.2%, and the Genetic Algorithm attained a confidence of 0.993 within realistic agronomic bounds. In an illustrative usability evaluation, the GenAI-UX interface obtained the highest System Usability Scale score (Good category). The results indicate that pairing accurate, interpretable models with a language-based delivery layer can transform complex sensor data into actionable irrigation recommendations, lowering the adoption barrier for non-technical users. Field validation with real respondents and edge deployment are identified as the next steps.
journal: Journal of Applied Informatics and Computing

title: Deep learning-based genetic disease prediction with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout uncertainty estimation: a comparative study with classical machine learning baselines
abstract: Background: Deep neural networks have been successfully applied to structured clinical data with a good predictive performance, but their point predictions do not reflect an indication of confidence, which limits their trustworthiness in screening for genetic conditions where an overconfident misclassification may delay the appropriate confirmatory testing or intervention. Methods: A feed-forward neural network (128-64-32 hidden units, batch normalization, and dropout p = 0.3) was trained to classify patients into five genetic-disease-associated groups based on twelve regularly accessible clinical and molecular biomarkers, using a publicly available, pre-labelled structured biomedical dataset (n = 1,000) whose real-world clinical vs. synthetic provenance could not be independently confirmed (see Section 2.1 and Limitations). Performance was assessed using stratified 5-fold cross-validation versus four traditional baselines (logistic regression, random forest, SVM, gradient boosting; McNemar’s test for pairwise significance). We quantified predictive uncertainty using Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout (T up to 200 stochastic passes), decomposed it into epistemic and aleatoric components, and evaluated it thru calibration analysis (ECE, MCE, Brier score, negative log-likelihood), an uncertainty-quality analysis (low/medium/high uncertainty strata), a selective-prediction (risk-coverage) analysis, a seven-configuration ablation study, and robustness testing across random seeds, reduced training data, and Gaussian feature noise. Results The developed network achieved 94.30% +- 1.36% cross-validated accuracy which was statistically comparable to logistic regression (p = 0.092) and gradient boosting (p = 0.238) but considerably inferior to random forest (95.50% +- 1.26%, p = 0.0018) and SVM (95.30% +- 1.36%, p = 0.0063). MC-Dropout obtained 93.33% accuracy (macro F1 = 0.933, macro ROC-AUC = 0.971, MCC = 0.917) with ECE = 0.076 on a held-out test partition—numerically the highest (worst) ECE among the six model/inference configurations evaluated, exceeding all four classical baselines (ECE 0.024–0.066), although MC-Dropout inference reduced negative log-likelihood substantially relative to deterministic inference (0.370 vs. 0.445), indicating its calibration benefit is concentrated in reducing the penalty for confident errors rather than in bin-wise confidence-accuracy alignment. Errors were about twice as likely in the highest (most uncertain) tercile of predictions than in the lowest (12.0% vs. 6.0% mistake rate), and 60% of all misclassifications were within the high-uncertainty group. Removing the most doubtful 20%–30% of predictions yielded a retained-sample accuracy of above 95%. Accuracy and calibration were consistent across five random seeds (93.07%) and deteriorated gracefully with increasing predictive entropy under synthetic feature-noise perturbation. Conclusion: On this structured, moderate-sized genetic-disease benchmark dataset—evaluated entirely through internal computational validation, without external or prospective clinical testing—classical machine learning algorithms achieved statistically comparable or slightly higher raw classification accuracy than this deep learning approach under standard, non-tuned hyperparameters for all models.

title: Towards digital agriculture: uncovering the drivers and barriers to the adoption of digital agricultural technologies
abstract: Accurately identifying the driving and hindering factors of agricultural digital technology adoption is the key to overcoming the “last mile” challenge in agricultural technology diffusion. Based on the evolutionary game theory of scale-free complex networks, this paper constructs an actor network for agricultural technology adoption to analyze its multidimensional mechanisms of influence in depth. The results indicate that while government subsidies provide short-term incentives for technology diffusion, their sustainability is limited. Agricultural technology advantages serve as the core driver, transforming exogenous technology into an endogenous growth engine. Conversely, the information gap, the perception of high risk, and high costs hinder farmers’ willingness to adopt these technologies. This study expands the application boundaries of complex network theory in agricultural technology adoption, reveals the operational laws governing driving and hindering factors, and provides a valuable reference for optimizing agricultural technology adoption strategies.

title: Do Machine Learning Models Beat a Constant Benchmark When Forecasting Next-Month Hurst Exponents? Evidence from Saudi-Listed Firms
abstract: Financial forecasting under uncertainty is fundamental to strategic investment decision making. Among the factors that influence investment decisions, market efficiency plays a critical role because it determines whether historical information can provide predictive value for future market behavior. The Hurst exponent is widely used to measure persistence and weak-form market efficiency, where values close to 0.5 indicate random behavior and values above or below 0.5 indicate persistent or mean-reverting dynamics. Despite extensive research using the Hurst exponent to characterize market persistence and market-efficiency-related behavior, limited studies have investigated whether future Hurst exponent estimates can be forecast using machine learning techniques and whether these models can outperform a simple constant benchmark. This study addresses this gap by developing a machine learning framework to forecast the next-month Hurst exponent using firm-level descriptive, financial, technical, and statistical indicators and comparing their performance against a constant benchmark. A dataset comprising 141 Saudi-listed companies, 705 firm-month observations, approximately 147 predictor variables, and five monthly periods was constructed. Monthly Hurst exponent values were estimated using the Rescaled Range (R/S) method and used as the target variable. Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Elastic Net, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated using an expanding-window time-series validation strategy with two chronological forecast origins. Model performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). None of the evaluated machine learning models outperformed the constant benchmark, which achieved the lowest RMSE (0.227) and MAE (0.179). Ridge Regression performed relatively best among the machine learning models, with an RMSE of 0.236 and an MAE of 0.187, but it still failed to improve upon the benchmark, and all evaluated machine learning models produced negative R2 values. These results indicate that the selected firm-level descriptive, financial, technical, and statistical indicators provided limited incremental forecasting value relative to a simple constant benchmark within the adopted empirical design. Given the five-month observation period and limited number of chronological forecast origins, the findings are best interpreted as exploratory evidence regarding the ability of machine learning models to outperform a constant benchmark in forecasting next-month Hurst estimates, rather than as definitive evidence concerning market efficiency or the general predictability of financial markets. The study provides an empirical benchmark for future investigations into forecasting Hurst exponent estimates and changes in market persistence.

title: Long-Term Dynamics of Ulva prolifera Blooms in the Yellow Sea and Their Environmental Associations: Insights from Multi-Source Remote Sensing
abstract: Recurrent Ulva prolifera (U. prolifera) green tides in the Yellow Sea have become a persistent coastal ecological problem, yet their long-term phenological changes and responses to environmental variability remain insufficiently understood. Here, we reconstructed the spatiotemporal dynamics of U. prolifera from 2008 to 2025 using multi-source satellite observations. Floating algae were detected using the Floating Algae Index (FAI) or Alternative Floating Algae Index (AFAI), and subpixel coverage was estimated using linear spectral unmixing. The results showed that MODIS-derived green tide extent expanded markedly, reaching 886.13 km2 in 2021. June exhibited the strongest long-term increasing trend. VIIRS observations showed broadly similar spatial and interannual bloom patterns over 2016–2025, while hourly GOCI-II observations revealed pronounced intraday variability which coverage generally increasing from morning to noon or afternoon. Environmental analyses demonstrated that bloom variability was jointly regulated by multiple environmental factors, including nonlinear relationships with sea surface temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen, as well as linear effects of salinity and silicate. The multivariable model explained 70.7% of the observed variation in bloom area, highlighting the importance of coupled physical and biogeochemical controls. These findings indicate that Yellow Sea green tides are becoming increasingly persistent under changing environmental conditions. Multi-source satellite monitoring can inform adaptive management that combines nature-based solutions (NbS), including source-region nutrient reduction, optimized aquaculture structures, ecological polyculture with competitive macroalgae, hydrodynamic-based interception, and sustainable biomass utilization. Such approaches may reduce bloom risks while enhancing coastal ecosystem resilience and transforming U. prolifera management from passive removal toward proactive ecological regulation.

title: QASHI: Quality-Aware Scale-Protected Hybrid Inference for Small-Object Detection in Optical and SAR Remote Sensing Imagery
abstract: Object detection in high-resolution remote sensing imagery faces a resolution–context trade-off: resizing weakens small objects, whereas cropping can truncate targets and remove context. We present QASHI, a detector-retraining-free hybrid inference framework combining a full-image view, four overlapping tiles, and at most three additional regions of interest (ROIs). Quality-Aware Density (QAD) prioritizes local re-inference by combining small-candidate density with weak responses, candidate competition, and full/tile prediction inconsistency. Graph-based ranking correction, bounded BoxVote refinement, and scale-protected routing integrate local predictions with full-image context. Experiments cover VisDrone2019-DET, DIOR, SeaDronesSee v2, and SRSDD-v1.0 with two RT-DETR detectors. On VisDrone-val with RT-DETRv4-S, QASHI improves AP by 2.84 points over the SAHI baseline while reducing mean latency by 14.40%. Relative to Full, it gains 5.74 AP points at 4.52 times the latency. Selector ablations and local parameter analyses characterize how region priority and fusion settings affect detection accuracy and computational cost. On SRSDD, display-domain image-quality sensitivity tests with RT-DETR-R50 yield higher mean perturbed AP (32.52 versus 31.41), with relative AP retention of 93.44% versus 93.98%. QASHI combines prediction-guided local processing and source-aware fusion to improve remote sensing detection through inference-time use of a fixed detector.

title: DMFNet: Phase-Enhanced Multi-Level Deformable Fusion for Multimodal Remote Sensing Classification
abstract: The collaborative classification of hyperspectral images (HSI) with a complementary modality such as light detection and ranging (LiDAR) or synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which is known as multi-source remote sensing image classification (MRSIC), can combine rich spectral information with structural cues and is helpful for the recognition of complex ground objects. However, effectively incorporating these structural cues into multi-level spectral-spatial features and modeling their spatial relationships remain challenging under limited training samples. To address these problems, a multi-level convolutional collaborative classification network based on the DefMamba fusion mechanism (DMFNet) is proposed in this paper. First, monogenic phase congruency (MPC) responses are added to the complementary modality to enhance its structural information. Then, a dual-branch feature extraction module is constructed to derive multi-level features from HSI and the enhanced complementary modality and aggregate them into a joint representation. Finally, a DefMamba fusion module applies deformable selective scanning to the aggregated features, so as to adaptively model spatial dependencies according to the fused content. Experiments on three public multimodal remote sensing datasets, covering both HSI–LiDAR and HSI–SAR settings, demonstrate that DMFNet achieves the highest mean overall accuracy among the compared methods with 10 labeled training samples per class, with the largest improvement on the HSI-SAR scene. Additional experiments on Houston 2018 further evaluate its classification performance on a large-scale scene.

title: Revealing the Hidden Archaeological Landscape of Ancient Colchis Using Multispectral and Thermal UAV Remote Sensing
abstract: This study investigates the potential of integrated multispectral and thermal UAV remote sensing for detecting and mapping hidden archaeological structures of Proto-Colchian and Colchian settlement systems of the 3rd–1st millennium BCE, within the Rioni River basin in western Georgia. Characteristic settlement mounds (Dikhagudzuba), moats/ditches, and possible paleochannel networks represent a unique example of large-scale adaptation to waterlogged environments, and limited archaeological excavations have significantly hindered the identification and interpretation of these buried landscape features. Pilot UAV surveys were conducted at four archaeological sites differing in location, geomorphological setting, land use, and degree of preservation using DJI Mavic 3M multispectral and DJI Matrice 4T thermal UAV platforms. Multispectral imagery enabled the detection of vegetation and soil-moisture anomalies associated with buried ditches, embankments, canals, and settlement structures, while thermal data revealed differences in thermal inertia related to subsurface archaeological remains and palaeohydrological features. The study covered approximately 15.4 ha and produced 5836 RGB, 2219 multispectral, and 3617 thermal images with spatial resolutions ranging from 1.87 to 4.61 cm. The integration of high-resolution elevation models, RGB imagery, vegetation indices (ExG and normalized EVI2), and thermal data enabled the identification and characterization of microtopographic, vegetation, moisture, and thermal anomalies associated with archaeological and palaeohydrological features. The investigated mounds cover 2754–4685 m2, reach approximately 9–10 m in height, and are surrounded by moats/ditches covering 4265–6520 m2 and ramparts reaching approximately 2–3.5 m in height. The results demonstrate that combined UAV-based multispectral and thermal remote sensing provides a highly effective non-invasive tool for archaeological prospection in dynamic wetland landscapes. The proposed approach significantly improves the detection of buried archaeological features and paleochannels, while also supporting landscape-scale analyses, monitoring of archaeological heritage, and the development of predictive archaeological models for western Georgia.

title: From Remote Sensing Accuracy to MRV Readiness: A Systematic Review and GeoAI Framework for Tropical Forest Biomass Estimation
abstract: Remote sensing combined with machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) is widely used to estimate tropical forest aboveground biomass (AGB), yet it is unclear how fully published studies document the evidence that Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) of forest carbon would require. We assessed this reporting evidence using a five-dimension framework (accuracy reporting, uncertainty quantification, spatial validation, temporal consistency and transparency) applied to a systematically identified set of empirical studies. From 1706 records retrieved from Scopus and Lens.org on 4 March 2026, 1146 unique works were screened against a locked eligibility codebook; 153 reports were assessed in full text where accessible, and 59 empirical ML/DL remote-sensing AGB studies in tropical or subtropical forests formed the core review set. For each dimension we coded evidence as confirmed, reported as absent, insufficient or inaccessible, and report the share of studies between the confirmed count and the confirmed-plus-undetermined count. Accuracy metrics were reported in 66–88% of studies, but spatially independent validation was confirmed in only 32–42%, spatially explicit or area-level uncertainty in 44–54%, multi-date analysis with an explicit consistency method in 14–22%, public code in 14–29% and public reference data in 15–29%. Only 12 studies confirmed both independent validation and propagated uncertainty. The results describe the evidence reported in research papers and do not assess compliance of any product with a carbon standard. Screening and evidence extraction were AI-assisted against a fixed codebook with a verbatim evidence phrase for every decision, and a stratified sample of 60 screening decisions was independently verified by two co-authors (agreement 88% and 78%). We recommend that biomass studies intended to inform MRV report spatially blocked or independent-site validation, propagate uncertainty to area totals, and release code and reference data.

title: A model of adaptive capacity through collective action in regional disaster mitigation governance in Mamuju Regency, West Sulawesi, Indonesia
abstract: Disaster mitigation governance increasingly requires attention to adaptive capacity as a process developed through interaction among actors rather than as a fixed set of resources or institutional attributes. In multihazard settings such as Mamuju Regency, West Sulawesi, this perspective helps explain how actors reorganise in response to disruption. This study examined how collective action contributed to adaptive capacity in local disaster mitigation governance in Mamuju Regency. This interpretive qualitative case study included 35 participants from disaster management agencies, local government institutions, volunteer organisations, and civil society. Data were generated through in-depth interviews, multistakeholder focus group discussions (FGDs), and institutional documents and analysed using thematic coding, interpretive reconstruction, and process tracing. Four interconnected mechanisms were identified: trust formation, adaptive coordination, social learning, and resource mobilisation. Their effects were visible in the reorganisation of communication and coordination during disruption. Adaptive capacity developed unevenly: absorptive capacity was most clearly observed, anticipatory capacity remained emerging, and transformative capacity was developing and conditional on the institutionalisation of learning and collaborative practices. Collective action did not automatically generate adaptive capacity; its contribution depended on whether interaction produced observable and sustained changes in preparedness, learning, coordination, and institutional adjustment. Contribution: The study provides a process-based explanation linking structural risk conditions, crisis-triggered interaction, collective-action mechanisms, adaptive outcomes, differentiated adaptive capacity, and governance adjustment.
